notes.b: Sport depends on athletes competing on equal terms. A drug that artificially lifts performance breaks that equal footing, so sport has a body and a list to control them.
points: A performance-enhancing drug (PED) is a substance taken to improve performance artificially, which gives the user an unfair advantage over athletes who do not take it.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) is the international body that fights drug use in sport. It publishes the Prohibited List, which is updated annually.
The Prohibited List names substances and methods (ways of improving performance that do not involve a drug). Each is banned at all times, banned in competition only, or banned in particular sports.
notes.tip: Creatine and caffeine at normal doses are not prohibited, so do not list them as PEDs. Keep drug categories separate from anti-doping rules, which are a different subsection.

notes.b: Anabolic agents are the drugs that build muscle. They are the PEDs most closely tied to strength and power, and they carry some of the widest health risks.
points: Examples: anabolic steroids (synthetic versions of male hormones) such as nandrolone, testosterone and stanozolol.
Effect: they increase protein synthesis (the body building new protein, which is what muscle is made of), so muscle mass, strength and power rise. This allows harder training and faster recovery.
Misused in strength and power events, because muscle mass and recovery from hard training matter most there.
Health risks: liver damage, heart disease, acne and aggression.
Hormonal effects: infertility, and masculinisation in women (developing male characteristics).
notes.tip: If asked for two effects of anabolic steroids on performance, give more muscle mass, strength and power, and faster recovery that allows harder training. For examples, name steroids such as nandrolone, testosterone or stanozolol.

notes.b: Hormones are chemical messengers made in the body. Peptide hormones and growth factors copy these messengers to change how the body performs and recovers. The two to know are EPO and HGH.
points: Erythropoietin (EPO) raises red blood cell production and oxygen-carrying capacity. More oxygen reaches the muscles, which improves endurance.
EPO is misused in endurance events such as distance running and cycling, because these events depend on a steady oxygen supply.
EPO health risks: thickened blood, which causes clots, stroke and heart attack.
Human growth hormone (HGH) increases muscle and aids recovery.
HGH health risks: abnormal growth and heart problems.
notes.tip: Exams ask for an example of a PED in the peptide hormones category, so name EPO or HGH. When describing how one affects performance, state the effect (EPO: oxygen-carrying capacity and endurance).

notes.b: Stimulants act on the body and brain to speed up and sharpen an athlete in the moment. They also hide the signals that would normally tell an athlete to slow down.
points: Examples: amphetamines, cocaine and ephedrine.
Effect: they increase alertness and aggression, and mask fatigue and pain (the athlete does not feel tiredness or pain that would normally force them to ease off).
Misused in sports that demand sustained alertness and aggression, such as contact sports and endurance events.
Health risks: high blood pressure, heart problems, overheating, addiction and poor judgement.
notes.tip: Stimulants are one of the categories exams ask you to give an example of. Name amphetamines, cocaine or ephedrine and state the effect.

notes.b: These drugs work by changing what leaves the body rather than by building performance directly. A diuretic is a drug that makes the body produce more urine.
points: Effect: they increase urine output. This allows rapid weight loss to make a weight category (the weight band an athlete must fit in to compete).
Masking agents work by diluting urine or otherwise hiding other drugs, so the athlete is less likely to be caught in a drug test.
Misused in weight-category sports such as boxing, because losing weight fast helps an athlete make the limit.
Health risks: dehydration, cramps and kidney problems.
notes.tip: When a table asks for a category with an example and its effect, link diuretics to rapid weight loss and to diluting or hiding other drugs.

notes.b: An analgesic is a painkiller. Narcotic analgesics are strong painkillers that let an athlete keep competing when the body is signalling injury.
points: Example: morphine.
Effect: it masks pain, so an athlete can compete while injured.
Misused in sports where athletes compete through injury, such as contact sports.
Health risks: worsening injury, because pain is the warning that stops an athlete using an injured body part, and addiction.
notes.tip: When describing how this category affects performance, say that it masks pain so the athlete can compete injured, then give the risk of worsening the injury.

notes.b: Beta-blockers calm the body, which is the opposite of a stimulant. That helps in sports where a steady hand matters more than power.
points: Effect: they lower heart rate and steady tremor (shaking of the hands), which helps precision performance.
They are prohibited in particular precision sports such as archery and shooting, where a steady hand decides the result.
Health risks: fatigue and low blood pressure.
notes.tip: Beta-blockers are banned in particular precision sports such as archery and shooting, so name the sport when you name them.

notes.h: Other drug classes on the list
notes.b: The Prohibited List is longer than the main categories above. Four more classes are on it.
points: Beta-2 agonists, hormone and metabolic modulators, cannabinoids and glucocorticoids are also on the Prohibited List.

notes.b: Not everything banned is a drug. Some banned methods change the body or the test result without a drug being taken.
points: Blood doping: a transfusion of blood to raise the red blood cell count, which carries more oxygen.
Tampering with samples, meaning interfering with the urine or blood sample given for testing.
Gene doping: altering genes to enhance performance.

notes.b: Athletes know the health and career risks, yet some still use PEDs. The reasons come from pressure and from the benefits a drug seems to offer.
points: Pressure to win, because success is what the athlete is judged on.
Financial rewards and sponsorship, which go to winners.
National pressure to succeed.
Belief that rivals are doping, so the athlete feels they must do the same to compete on equal terms.
Recovering from injury faster, so they can return to training and competition sooner.
Making a weight category.
Ageing athletes trying to stay competitive as their natural performance declines.
notes.tip: Exams ask why an athlete might use a PED. Give a reason and develop it, for example financial reward or the belief that rivals are doping.

notes.b: An athlete who is caught, or who simply takes PEDs, faces consequences in their health, their results, their income and their name. Each is a separate implication you can use in an answer.
points: Health: short- and long-term risks from the categories above, including death in extreme cases.
Sanctions: a ban, normally four years for intentional doping, and disqualification of results.
Losses: medals and records are taken away.
Financial and career: loss of funding, prize money and sponsorship, and the career can end.
Reputation and personal: public disgrace, damage to family, mental-health effects and loss of self-respect.
notes.tip: Exams ask for implications for the performer with examples. Use the health risks of a named drug, a ban, and loss of medals, income or reputation. Do not invent statistics on positive tests.

notes.b: Doping harms more than the individual. When rules are broken, the whole activity pays, from public trust to the clean athletes who compete against dopers.
points: Credibility: public trust falls, and every outstanding performance is doubted.
Commercial: sponsors, broadcasters and spectators withdraw, which reduces funding.
Clean athletes (those who do not dope) lose medals, places and earnings, and records may be reallocated years later.
Participation: young people and parents turn away, and others may feel pressure to dope.
Cost and exclusion: testing and education are expensive, and a country or team may be excluded from competition.
notes.tip: To examine the idea that doping damages the sport, cover credibility, loss of sponsors and spectators, cheated clean athletes, falling participation, and the cost of testing and education.

keyTerms.definition: A substance taken to improve performance artificially, giving an unfair advantage.
The list, published by WADA each year, of substances and methods banned in sport.
A drug, such as an anabolic steroid, that increases protein synthesis, muscle mass and strength.
A peptide hormone that raises red blood cell production and oxygen-carrying capacity.
A peptide hormone that increases muscle and aids recovery.
A drug that increases alertness and aggression and masks fatigue and pain.
A drug that increases urine output.
A substance used to dilute or hide other drugs in a sample.
A drug, such as morphine, that masks pain.
A drug that lowers heart rate and steadies tremor, and is prohibited in particular sports such as archery and shooting.
The transfusion of blood to raise the red blood cell count.
The altering of genes to enhance performance.

factCards.term: Two effects of anabolic steroids on performance
factCards.definition: They increase protein synthesis, muscle mass, strength and power, and allow harder training and faster recovery.
Thickened blood, clots, stroke and heart attack.
Particular precision sports, such as archery and shooting.

factCards.term: Two implications of doping for the sport
factCards.definition: Loss of public trust, with every outstanding performance doubted; loss of sponsors, broadcasters and spectators.

questions.prompt: Describe three categories of performance-enhancing drugs, naming an example of each and its effect on performance.
questions.model: 1. Anabolic agents: for example nandrolone or testosterone. They increase protein synthesis, muscle mass and strength, so an athlete can train harder and recover faster, which matters in strength and power events. 2. Peptide hormones: for example erythropoietin (EPO). EPO raises red blood cell production and oxygen-carrying capacity, improving endurance in events such as distance running and cycling. 3. Stimulants: for example amphetamines. They increase alertness and aggression and mask fatigue and pain, so an athlete can push on for longer, but they raise blood pressure and add the risk of heart problems and overheating.

questions.prompt: Analyse the implications for the performer and for the sport of using performance-enhancing drugs.
questions.model: For the performer, health is at risk, from short-term effects to long-term damage such as heart and liver problems, and in extreme cases death. A violation can bring a ban, normally four years for intentional doping, and disqualification of results, with medals and records taken away. The athlete can lose funding, prize money and sponsorship, and face public disgrace, damage to family and mental-health effects, so a career can end. For the sport, public trust falls and every outstanding performance is doubted. Sponsors, broadcasters and spectators withdraw, reducing funding. Clean athletes lose medals, places and earnings, and records may be reallocated years later. Young people and parents may turn away from the sport, and others may feel pressure to dope.

questions.prompt: Name two PEDs and describe a negative effect of each on the athlete.
questions.model: 1. Anabolic steroids: they can cause liver damage and heart disease, and in women they cause masculinisation. 2. Erythropoietin (EPO): it thickens the blood, raising the risk of clots, stroke and heart attack.
